questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to train a dog to help people in danger
Whether pets notice and care about our feelings
Why cats make better pets than dogs
The history of animal shows on children's TV
questions.why: Neil asks whether in real life animals know, or care, about human feelings, and they discuss an experiment.

questions.q: What does Sam remember about the TV show 'Lassie'?
options: Lassie was a cat that lived with a family
Lassie often got lost and Timmy found her
Lassie could talk to Timmy like a human
Lassie sensed danger and rescued Timmy
questions.why: Sam says whenever Timmy got into trouble, Lassie sensed danger and came to the rescue.

questions.q: According to Neil, why is it easy to misunderstand our pets?
options: They can't tell us how they feel
They hide their feelings on purpose
They only care about getting food
They behave differently when we're out
questions.why: Neil says pets can't talk to say how they're feeling, which makes it easy to misunderstand them.

questions.q: What did Dr Karen Hiestand's experiment involve?
options: Leaving pets alone in the house for a day
Giving pets different kinds of food
Filming owners pretending to be hurt
Asking pets to follow simple commands
questions.why: She filmed pet owners pretending to be hurt and observed how their dogs and cats reacted.

questions.q: What did Adrian Washbourne think of his pets' reaction to his fake injury?
options: They were very worried and ran to help him
They didn't seem very bothered
They were frightened and ran away
They were angry and started barking
questions.why: He says, 'I don't think they were particularly sensitive or bothered' – the dog yawned, the cat just stared.

questions.q: Why does Dr Hiestand think dogs come closer to investigate?
options: They come from wolves, which live in packs
They are hoping to be given some food
They have been trained to help humans
They are much more intelligent than cats
questions.why: Dogs are descended from wolves – very social animals living in packs – so they come closer to investigate.

questions.q: How did cats typically react when their owner seemed upset?
options: They ran to another room to hide
They came and sat on their owner
They walked around and made noises
They stayed still and watched closely
questions.why: She says cats stayed much more still, looking at their owner and paying them a lot of attention.

questions.q: What do Dr Hiestand's findings suggest about cats?
options: They don't notice human feelings at all
They care about people more than dogs do
They sense distress but show it differently
They only care about their own feelings
questions.why: Neil says her findings show cats also feel human distress – 'they just show it in a different way'.
